## Livestock Farmers on a Tightrope: Pastures Emerging Early and Growing Scarce

At seven in the morning, as the sun barely peeks over the Veleta, José Miguel Rodríguez opens the gate to the sheepfold and watches the herd with the unease of someone who has been doing the math for months and finding it doesn't add up. He is a Malagueña goat breeder in Capileira and a member of the Asociación de Ganaderos de la Alpujarra, a network of producers documenting changes in pasture cycles with the precision of a field notebook. His goats, accustomed to vertical transhumance between 1,000 and 2,500 meters, no longer find what they used to when they climbed the mountains in search of the tender June shoots.

The problem, according to data from the Red de Pastos de Andalucía, is that the available biomass in high-altitude pastures has decreased by 15 percent since the year 2000. This is not an abstract figure: in the Valle del Poqueira, it translates to hillsides yellowing ahead of schedule, herds returning to the pens with half-empty stomachs, and farmers having to buy feed in the middle of summer—something unthinkable two decades ago. Pastures sprout earlier, driven by increasingly warmer springs, but they also dry out sooner, punished by summers that grow longer and tighten their grip with an intensity unknown to the oldest shepherds in the region.

Vertical transhumance, that millennial movement that took herds from the temperate valleys to the cool peaks of Sierra Nevada, has been shortened by three weeks. This is confirmed by the records of the livestock association and studies from the Universidad de Córdoba, which monitors the Alpujarra pastures with sampling stations distributed across the entire southern slope. Previously, the goats and sheep would go up in mid-June and remain in the high mountains well into September. Now the ascent is delayed because the mid-slope pastures are still holding up, but the descent is brought forward because there is nothing left to eat up above.

María Dolores Haro, a veterinarian at the Universidad de Córdoba specializing in extensive livestock systems, explains that the mismatch affects not only the quantity of pasture but also its nutritional quality. Grasses and legumes that grow in early heat develop less protein and more fiber, forcing animals to consume more dry matter to obtain the same energy. Segureña sheep, a hardy breed adapted to the harshness of these mountains, cope better than others, but even they are feeling the change. Farmers notice it in milk production, lamb weight, and female fertility—indicators that suffer season after season.

The Valle del Poqueira concentrates some of the most evident cases of this transformation. In Pampaneira, Bubión, and Capileira, herds of Malagueña goats share the communal pastures with Segureña sheep in a delicate balance that the climate is destabilizing. The younger shepherds, those who inherited the trade from their fathers, speak of a calendar that no longer works: the dates for going up and coming down that they learned as children have become obsolete. Now they have to improvise, read the mountain week by week, decide on the fly whether it is worth going up or waiting, whether it pays to rent pastures in other areas, or whether it is better to reduce the herd.

The reduction in biomass is not uniform throughout the region. Studies by the Red de Pastos de Andalucía show that the most affected areas are precisely those at the highest altitudes, those that depend on snowmelt to maintain soil moisture during the summer. With scarcer snowfall and an advancing spring, the water available for summit pastures decreases just when it is needed most. The snowfields that once lasted until August in the shaded slopes of Mulhacén now disappear weeks earlier, and with them vanishes the water reserve that fed the July and August pastures.

The livestock farmers of the Alpujarra know the paradox they have to live with all too well. While rural tourism celebrates the extension of good weather and visitors fill the trails in months that used to be snow and mud, they watch as the very phenomenon that delights hoteliers ruins their pastures. The region suffers from a sort of climate schizophrenia: what for some is an extended high season is for others a silent disaster measured in kilos of purchased feed and animals that do not reach the slaughterhouse at optimal weight.

The Asociación de Ganaderos de la Alpujarra has begun collecting its own testimonies and data to document what it considers a livestock emergency. In their assemblies, held in the back rooms of some bar in Bubión or in the municipal halls of Capileira, the same questions are repeated: how much longer can vertical transhumance be maintained? What alternatives exist for a production system that depends on a natural cycle that is breaking down? Some members have chosen to reduce their headcount, others to diversify with the direct sale of cheese and suckling lamb, and a few have abandoned the activity altogether, unable to sustain a business that demands more investment each year and yields less return.

Data from the Universidad de Córdoba suggest that biomass loss could accelerate in the coming years if the observed temperature and precipitation trends continue. Climate models for Sierra Nevada anticipate longer, drier summers, with a significant reduction in snow cover at the peaks. For the shepherds of the Poqueira, this means the margin for adaptation is narrowing: it is no longer enough to adjust the dates of transhumance, because high-altitude pasture is ceasing to be a reliable resource. The question hanging in the air is whether mountain extensive livestock farming, that trade that has shaped the Alpujarra landscape for centuries, can survive a climate that is changing faster than the herds' capacity to adapt.

Meanwhile, every morning José Miguel Rodríguez continues to open the gate to the sheepfold and look toward the mountains, hoping the terrain will hold out for one more week. His goats, oblivious to the statistics, search among the stones for the last green shoots remaining in the shaded areas. The sound of their bells echoes through the valley as a reminder that the Alpujarra is not just a landscape to be photographed, but a living territory where the climate writes a daily story of resistance and loss.
